s: A company hosts an ecommerce site using EC2, ALB, and DynamoDB in one AWS Region. The site uses a custom domain in Route 53. The company wants to replicate the stack to a second Region for disaster recovery and faster access for global customers. What should the architect do?
o: Use CloudFormation to deploy to the second Region. Use Route 53 latency-based routing. Enable global tables in DynamoDB.
Use the console to recreate the infra manually in the second Region. Use weighted routing.
Replicate only the S3 and DynamoDB data. Use Route 53 failover routing.
Use Beanstalk and DynamoDB Streams for replication. Use latency-based routing.
e: A is correct because: CloudFormation templates enable repeatable infrastructure deployment. Route 53 latency-based routing ensures users hit the closest Region. DynamoDB global tables allow multi-Region, active-active replication of application data. Manual console work (B) is not scalable. C lacks EC2/ALB replication. D adds unnecessary services like Beanstalk and doesn't scale cleanly. Reference:https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GlobalTables.ht ml

w.y: "Disaster recovery" plus "faster access for global customers" decide it. CloudFormation repeats the stack reliably in the second Region, Route 53 latency-based routing sends users to the nearer Region, and DynamoDB global tables replicate data both ways.

o.A: Correct: IaC copy of the stack, latency routing, and DynamoDB global tables.
o.B: Manual rebuilding is error-prone, and weighted routing does not send users to the closest Region.
o.C: Failover routing gives DR but not faster access, and the app stack is not replicated.
o.D: Building your own replication with DynamoDB Streams is more work than global tables.
